questions.q: A 35-year-old farmer presents with a painless papule on the dorsum of his right hand that evolved into an ulcer with a black eschar surrounded by extensive non-pitting oedema. He has no fever. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Cutaneous anthrax (malignant pustule) presents as a painless papule progressing to a necrotic ulcer with a black eschar (due to Bacillus anthracis exotoxin) with surrounding non-pitting gelatinous oedema. The absence of pain is a hallmark feature distinguishing it from other infections.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with recurrent grouped vesicles on an erythematous base on her lip, preceded by tingling. PCR confirms HSV-1. She has 6 recurrences per year. The most appropriate long-term management is:
questions.exp: Suppressive therapy with acyclovir 400mg twice daily is recommended when a patient has 6 or more recurrences per year. It reduces recurrence frequency by 70-80%. Episodic therapy is used for fewer than 6 recurrences per year. Topical agents are less effective and famciclovir single dose is for episodic use.

questions.q: A 22-year-old male presents with annular plaques with central hypopigmentation on the trunk, reduced sensation on the plaques, and a thickened right ulnar nerve. Slit-skin smear is negative. Lepromin test shows 8mm induration at 4 weeks. What is the classification?
questions.exp: Borderline tuberculoid (BT) leprosy features few asymmetric hypopigmented plaques with impaired sensation, peripheral nerve involvement (ulnar), negative SSS (paucibacillary), and a positive Mitsuda (lepromin) reaction >5mm at 28 days indicating cell-mediated immunity. BT is classified as paucibacillary.

questions.q: A 45-year-old diabetic woman develops a rapidly spreading necrotic wound on her left vulva with crepitus and foul-smelling discharge, followed by fever and septic shock. Imaging shows gas in soft tissue planes. The pathognomonic feature of this condition is:
opts: Gas in fascial planes on imaging
questions.exp: Fournier's gangrene is a type of necrotizing fasciitis involving the perineum/genitalia. The pathognomonic feature is gas in fascial planes on imaging (CT/X-ray), produced by synergistic polymicrobial infection (aerobic and anaerobic bacteria including Clostridium). Haemorrhagic bullae can occur but are not pathognomonic.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man presents with well-defined hyperpigmented plaques with fine scaling on the chest and back. KOH mount shows 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance. Hypopigmented lesions in pityriasis versicolor are caused by Malassezia producing which substance that inhibits tyrosinase?
questions.exp: Pityriasis versicolor is caused by Malassezia furfur. Hypopigmented lesions occur because Malassezia produces azelaic acid (a dicarboxylic acid from oleic acid oxidation), which inhibits tyrosinase, reducing melanin synthesis. The 'spaghetti and meatballs' pattern (hyphae and spores) is diagnostic on KOH.

questions.q: A 25-year-old sexually active man presents with a painless indurated ulcer on his glans penis with a clean base and firm non-tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. VDRL is reactive 1:8. The most accurate confirmatory test in the primary stage is:
questions.exp: Primary syphilis: Dark-field microscopy of ulcer exudate (demonstrating Treponema pallidum motility) is the most direct and accurate test when the ulcer is present. FTA-ABS is a confirmatory treponemal test but requires serology. VDRL/RPR are non-treponemal and can have false positives. Dark-field is the gold standard in primary chancre.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman presents with tense blisters on normal-appearing skin and urticarial plaques on the flexures. Nikolsky sign is negative. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 at the dermoepidermal junction. The autoantigen targeted is:
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid: autoantibodies target BP180 (BPAG2, type XVII collagen) and BP230 (BPAG1) in the hemidesmosome. DIF shows linear IgG/C3 at the DEJ. Tense blisters on normal/urticarial skin with negative Nikolsky sign distinguishes it from pemphigus. Desmoglein 3/1 are targeted in pemphigus. Type VII collagen is the antigen in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man with long-standing psoriasis develops new widespread erythema covering >90% BSA with scaling, fever, and chills after abruptly stopping oral methotrexate. What is the most feared systemic complication of erythroderma?
questions.exp: Erythrodermic psoriasis (>90% BSA involvement) leads to massive vasodilation causing high-output cardiac failure, thermoregulatory failure, protein loss, and electrolyte imbalance. It can be triggered by abrupt withdrawal of systemic therapy. High-output cardiac failure is the most life-threatening complication.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman presents with malar rash, photosensitivity, arthralgia, and positive ANA (1:640). Anti-dsDNA antibodies are strongly positive. Which antibody-complication pairing is most accurate?
questions.exp: Anti-dsDNA antibodies are highly specific for SLE (>95% specificity) and their titres correlate with disease activity, particularly lupus nephritis. Anti-Ro/SSA is associated with neonatal lupus and subacute cutaneous lupus. Anti-Sm is specific but not sensitive for SLE. Anti-histone antibodies are seen in drug-induced lupus.

questions.q: A 65-year-old man presents with a pearly, translucent nodule with telangiectasia on his nose that has central ulceration (rodent ulcer). Which molecular pathway is primarily dysregulated in this tumour?
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC): The Hedgehog signalling pathway is the primary dysregulated pathway. Loss-of-function mutations in PTCH1 (tumour suppressor) or gain-of-function mutations in SMO lead to constitutive Hedgehog pathway activation. Vismodegib and sonidegib are SMO inhibitors used for advanced BCC. 'Rodent ulcer' is a classic term for BCC.

questions.q: A 28-year-old man with HIV (CD4 200/uL) presents with extensive papular lesions with central umbilication on the face and genitalia, some measuring up to 2cm. For large solitary lesions, the most definitive treatment is:
questions.exp: Molluscum contagiosum in HIV/immunocompromised patients presents as giant molluscum (>2cm) and extensive lesions. For large individual lesions, curettage and electrodesiccation provides definitive mechanical removal. Cryotherapy is effective for small/moderate lesions. Imiquimod works via immune modulation but is slower. Intralesional cidofovir is reserved for recalcitrant cases.

questions.q: A 5-year-old child presents with golden-crusted lesions around the mouth and nose. Culture grows S. aureus producing exfoliative toxin. This toxin causes superficial blister formation by cleaving which protein?
questions.exp: Bullous impetigo is caused by S. aureus phage group II producing exfoliative toxins (ET-A, ET-B), which are serine proteases that specifically cleave desmoglein 1 (Dsg1) in the granular layer of the epidermis. This is the same mechanism as staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) but localised in bullous impetigo.

questions.q: An immunosuppressed renal transplant patient develops painful dermatomal vesicular eruption on the left T5 dermatome and subsequently develops contralateral hemiplegia. The mechanism of this neurological complication is:
opts: VZV granulomatous angiitis of cerebral vessels
questions.exp: Herpes zoster (VZV reactivation) can cause contralateral hemiplegia (cerebral granulomatous angiitis) particularly with ophthalmic zoster, due to VZV vasculitis of cerebral vessels via retrograde spread from the trigeminal ganglion to the circle of Willis. This is the most feared neurological complication of HZO.

questions.q: A 38-year-old woman presents with erythematous plaques on her elbows, knees, and scalp with silvery scales. Auspitz sign is positive. Which histopathological finding is characteristic of active psoriasis?
opts: Munro microabscesses and Kogoj spongiform pustules
questions.exp: Psoriasis histopathology: Munro microabscesses (neutrophil collections in stratum corneum) and Kogoj spongiform pustules (neutrophils in upper spinous layer) are characteristic. Other features include parakeratosis, elongated rete ridges, suprapapillary thinning, and dilated tortuous capillaries. Spongiosis with eosinophils suggests eczema; Civatte bodies suggest lichen planus.

questions.q: A 52-year-old woman presents with dysphagia, Raynaud's phenomenon, tight skin over the fingers extending to the forearms, and telangiectasia. ANA shows a centromere pattern. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (lcSSc/CREST): characterised by Calcinosis, Raynaud's, oEsophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia. Skin involvement is limited to distal extremities and face. Anti-centromere antibodies (ACA) are highly specific for lcSSc. Diffuse SSc has anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) and more extensive skin and visceral involvement.

questions.q: A 23-year-old woman presents with painful genital ulcers with ragged undermined edges, non-indurated margins, and tender fluctuant inguinal buboes. Gram stain of bubo aspirate shows a 'school of fish' pattern. Treatment of choice is:
opts: Benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU IM single dose
questions.exp: Chancroid (Haemophilus ducreyi): painful soft ulcer with ragged undermined edges, non-indurated, bleeds easily, with tender inguinal buboes. 'School of fish' or 'railroad tracks' on Gram stain reflects H. ducreyi's arrangement. Treatment: Azithromycin 1g single dose OR ceftriaxone 250mg IM single dose. Doxycycline is for LGV; penicillin for syphilis.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man presents with tense blisters predominantly on the oral mucosa and skin, positive Nikolsky sign, positive Tzanck smear showing acantholytic cells. Direct IF shows intercellular IgG in a 'chicken wire' pattern. The autoantigen is:
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris: autoantibodies target Desmoglein 3 (Dsg3), predominantly expressed in the oral mucosa and lower epidermis. Oral lesions predominate when only anti-Dsg3 is present. When both anti-Dsg3 and anti-Dsg1 are present, skin and mucous membrane lesions occur. Positive Nikolsky sign, acantholysis, and intercellular IgG DIF are diagnostic.

questions.q: During punch biopsy, the punch is inserted with a rotational motion. To achieve optimal wound closure and cosmesis, the elliptical defect should be oriented parallel to:
questions.exp: When performing punch biopsy, the punch should be oriented parallel to Relaxed Skin Tension Lines (RSTL) to achieve optimal wound closure and cosmesis. RSTL are perpendicular to underlying muscle action and provide the best cosmetic outcome for linear closure. Langer's lines are used for surgical incisions and approximate RSTL but are less precise.

questions.q: A 16-year-old boy is prescribed isotretinoin for severe nodular acne. The most important monitoring parameters during therapy include:
opts: CBC with differential and serum creatinine
Fasting lipid profile and liver function tests
Thyroid function tests and serum creatinine
questions.exp: Isotretinoin (13-cis-retinoic acid) monitoring requires fasting lipid profile (triglycerides, LDL, HDL) and liver function tests (AST, ALT) before therapy and at 1 month, then every 3 months. Isotretinoin causes dose-dependent hypertriglyceridaemia (in up to 25%) and can elevate liver enzymes. Pregnancy test (urine/serum beta-hCG) is mandatory for females (iPLEDGE programme).

questions.q: A 42-year-old woman presents with violaceous flat-topped polygonal papules on the flexor aspects of the wrists with Wickham's striae, and reticular white streaks on the buccal mucosa. Histology shows 'saw-tooth' rete ridges. The mechanism of keratinocyte damage is:
opts: IgG-mediated complement activation at the DEJ
CD8+ cytotoxic T-cell attack on basal keratinocytes
Mast cell degranulation and IgE-mediated reaction
questions.exp: Lichen planus: CD8+ cytotoxic T-lymphocytes attack basal keratinocytes expressing altered surface antigens, leading to vacuolar degeneration of the basal layer, Civatte bodies (apoptotic keratinocytes), and a 'saw-tooth' rete ridge pattern with band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the DEJ. Wickham's striae represent focal hypergranulosis.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man presents with a 2cm hyperpigmented macule on his palm present since childhood. Dermoscopy reveals a parallel ridge pattern on the skin markings. The most appropriate next step is:
opts: Punch biopsy from the darkest area only
questions.exp: Parallel ridge pattern on dermoscopy of acral lesions is a criterion for acral lentiginous melanoma with high PPV (>86%). Parallel furrow pattern (following skin furrows/sulci) is benign (acral melanocytic naevus). A parallel ridge pattern (on crests) warrants excision biopsy with adequate margins as the standard management for clinically/dermoscopically suspicious acral lesions.

questions.q: A 55-year-old farmer from Maharashtra presents with painless verrucous nodular lesions on the foot that slowly spread over 10 years. Histopathology reveals 'Medlar bodies' (sclerotic bodies). The most appropriate treatment is:
questions.exp: Chromoblastomycosis is caused by dematiaceous fungi (Fonsecaea pedrosoi most common in India). Pathognomonic: 'Medlar bodies' (copper-penny bodies/sclerotic bodies) — thick-walled muriform cells on histology. Treatment: Itraconazole 200-400mg/day is first-line; combination with terbinafine improves outcomes for extensive disease. Griseofulvin is for dermatophytosis only.

questions.q: A neonate develops blistering at sites of minor trauma, sparing mucous membranes. Electron microscopy shows cleavage at the level of the lamina lucida. The mutation responsible is most likely in:
opts: Laminin-332 or alpha-6/beta-4 integrin or type XVII collagen
questions.exp: Junctional EB (JEB): cleavage occurs within the lamina lucida of the basement membrane zone. Mutations are in LAMA3, LAMB3, LAMC2 (laminin-332), ITGA6, ITGB4 (alpha6beta4 integrin), or COL17A1 (type XVII collagen/BP180). Keratin 5/14 mutations cause EB simplex (intraepidermal). Type VII collagen mutations cause dystrophic EB (sublamina densa).

questions.q: A 48-year-old man presents with multiple yellowish papules around the eyes and along tendons with serum cholesterol of 380mg/dL. Histology shows sheets of foam cells. The underlying receptor deficiency in familial hypercholesterolaemia is:
questions.exp: Xanthomas in familial hypercholesterolaemia result from LDL receptor (LDLR) mutations, causing impaired LDL uptake by cells. Elevated serum LDL leads to macrophage foam cell formation in skin (xanthelasma, plane xanthomas) and tendons (tendinous xanthomas). FH is autosomal dominant; homozygotes develop xanthomas in childhood.

questions.q: A 19-year-old presents with painful oral aphthous ulcers recurring 3-4 times per year, recurrent genital ulcers, and hypopyon uveitis. Pathergy test is positive. What is the HLA association of this condition?
questions.exp: Behcet's disease: characterised by recurrent oral aphthous ulcers, genital ulcers, ocular involvement (hypopyon uveitis), skin lesions (pseudofolliculitis, erythema nodosum, pathergy). HLA-B51 is the strongest genetic association, particularly in patients from the Silk Road region. HLA-B27 is with ankylosing spondylitis; HLA-DR4 with rheumatoid arthritis; HLA-Cw6 with psoriasis.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man has hypopigmented macules on the face and extremities since childhood. Wood's lamp shows ivory white fluorescence. Biopsy shows complete absence of melanocytes. To differentiate this from piebaldism, the most definitive investigation is:
opts: Genetic testing for KIT gene mutation
Skin biopsy electron microscopy for melanosomes
questions.exp: Piebaldism is a rare autosomal dominant genodermatosis caused by KIT gene (or SLUG/SNAI2) mutations, presenting at birth with a stable white forelock and midline depigmented patches. Genetic testing for KIT mutations confirms piebaldism. Both vitiligo and piebaldism show absent melanocytes on biopsy and negative DOPA reaction; congenital onset and stable nature distinguish piebaldism clinically.

questions.q: A 26-year-old woman presents with pruritic papules and vesicles over extensor surfaces, scalp, and buttocks, with chronic diarrhoea. IgA endomysial antibodies are positive. DIF shows granular IgA deposits at the tips of dermal papillae. Treatment is:
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (Duhring's disease) is associated with coeliac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy) and IgA endomysial/tissue transglutaminase antibodies. Granular IgA at dermal papilla tips on DIF is pathognomonic. Treatment: strict gluten-free diet (definitive, treats both skin and gut) plus dapsone (rapid symptom control, 50-100mg/day). Dapsone does not alter intestinal pathology.

questions.q: During Mohs micrographic surgery for sclerosing BCC on the nose, horizontal frozen sections are used. The key advantage of Mohs surgery over standard wide local excision is:
opts: Faster procedure with no need for anaesthesia
100% of the surgical margins are examined histologically
Zero recurrence rate in all cases
Can be performed for all types of melanoma
questions.exp: Mohs micrographic surgery's unique advantage is 100% margin examination (both peripheral and deep margins via horizontal sectioning of the entire excised tissue), compared to WLE where only 1-2% of margins are sampled by bread-loaf sectioning. This allows complete tumour removal with maximal tissue conservation, achieving 5-year cure rates of up to 99% for primary BCC.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man on long-term hydroxychloroquine for discoid lupus develops progressive visual field defects. Ophthalmology detects 'bull's eye maculopathy'. The mechanism of hydroxychloroquine retinal toxicity is:
opts: Accumulation in RPE causing lysosomal dysfunction and photoreceptor damage
Direct mitochondrial toxicity in ganglion cells
questions.exp: Hydroxychloroquine retinopathy: the drug accumulates in melanin-containing cells of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and binds to melanin, causing lysosomal dysfunction and photoreceptor damage. The 'bull's eye maculopathy' pattern results from paracentral rod/cone damage with foveal sparing. Risk factors: cumulative dose >5mg/kg/day, duration >5 years. Baseline and annual ophthalmology screening are mandatory.

questions.q: A 3-year-old boy presents with ichthyosis-like skin, recurrent bacterial infections, partial oculocutaneous albinism, and giant lysosomal granules in neutrophils on peripheral smear. The mutated gene encodes:
questions.exp: Chediak-Higashi syndrome (CHS): autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in LYST gene (CHS1, chromosome 1q42), encoding a lysosomal trafficking regulator. Results in giant lysosomal granules in all granule-containing cells (neutrophils, melanocytes, NK cells, platelets), causing partial albinism, recurrent pyogenic infections (neutrophil dysfunction), and bleeding tendency. Filaggrin mutations cause ichthyosis vulgaris/atopic dermatitis.

questions.q: A 47-year-old woman presents with painless swelling of the labia majora of 4 months' duration and extensive matted groin lymphadenopathy. Complement fixation test titre is 1:64. The causative Chlamydia trachomatis serovars are:
opts: D, E, F, G, H, I, J, K
questions.exp: Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1, L2, L3. Characterised by a painless primary papule (often missed), followed by inguinal lymphadenopathy (groove sign — Poupart's ligament divides inguinal nodes), and late genital elephantiasis (esthiomene). CFT >1:64 is diagnostic. Serovars D-K cause urogenital chlamydial infection; A-C cause ocular trachoma.
